newsitem.title: UK: BAA not losing hope for Heathrow terminal five.
newsitem.headline: BAA not losing hope for Heathrow terminal five.

text.p: British airports operator BAA Plc denied on Friday that a change in accounting policy meant it now feared that a project to build a giant passenger terminal at London Heathrow might be blocked.
A lengthy planning inquiry has delayed the 1.5 billion pound ($2.4 billion) project for a fifth terminal.

BAA conceded that the delays meant the new terminal, which is designed to increase Heathrow's current capacity by 50 percent, would not now open until 2004 at the earliest, two years later than it had originally planned.
Delays in completing the marathon public inquiry had forced the company to stop capitalising interest on preparatory spending, it said.
As a result it said that it would book in a 40 million pound exceptional interest charge in its results for the year to March 31 1997, to write off the accumulated interest previously capitalised.
It also said it would be increasing its interest charges in the profit and loss account by 13 million pounds to take account of the amount that would otherwise have been capitalised this year.

"It's not a lack of confidence on our part," finance director Russell Walls told Reuters. "It's just that with the delay this (capitalised interest) is becoming 30 percent of the total amount (spent) and it's compounding all the time."

The public inquiry opened in May 1995 but a long queue of environmental groups, local authorities and residents wanting to give evidence means the public planning inspector does not expect to complete hearings until mid-1998.
BAA said on Friday it therefore did not now expect a government decision on the project until early in the year 2000.

The company said that it would resume capitalising interest on the project if and when planning permission was granted. But it now does not expect to get planning permission until the turn of the century.
So far BAA has spent 178 million pounds on preparatory work, including site preparation, design work, and making its case at the planning inquiry, of which 49 million pounds was capitalised interest.

BAA said that only interest charges would be affected, and the development costs themselves which were currently running at around 30 million pounds a year would continue to be capitalised, demonstrating that BAA remained confident of getting the project approved eventually.

"It just seemed to me that this was going on too long and with planning permission not now expected until the end of the century this interest was just going to roll up and roll up and roll up," said Walls.
"There would be too much capitalised interest sitting on this project," he added.
"We reckon that the Inspector is likely to take a year to write his report and then the secretaries of state for transport and environment have to make their decision."
"If it took (another) six months for a decision that would be pretty good going," he said.

But it remains to be seen whether BAA could meet its revised schedule to open the first phase of the development in the year 2004. "If we get permission by the end of the century we can have the first phase open before the end of 2004," Walls said.

BAA announced on Thursday that it had agreed with British Airways that the British flag carrier and its alliance partners would get the fifth terminal and give up Terminal One to the rival alliance grouping of United Airlines, Lufthansa, SAS, Air Canada and Thai Airways.
Last year, Heathrow handled nearly 56 million passengers but BAA and its airlines say the airport is now close to full capacity.
BAA's share price was down seven pence at 525 by 1000 GMT on Friday, bouncing back from an earlier low of 521p after analysts had assessed the news.

Mike Powell of NatWest Markets said that in making the move BAA was deferring to some concern from investors and analysts that interest should not be capitalised on a project that was not yet approved.
